newsitem.title: USA: J.P. Morgan EMBI+ index off 3.61 pct in March.
newsitem.headline: J.P. Morgan EMBI+ index off 3.61 pct in March.

text.p: J.P. Morgan & Co Inc said Thursday that its Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus (EMBI+) fell 3.61 percent in March, reducing its first quarter gain to 0.78 percent.
"Volatility increased as the market dealt with the liklihood of a Fed (Federal Reserve) rate increase and the possibility of further rate hikes in 1997," the company said.

All EMBI-plus countries posted losses in March, causing EMBI sovereign spreads to widen by 71 basis points to close at 507 basis points after nearly reaching its historic low of 392 basis points in February, it said.
The EMBI+ tracks total returns for traded external debt instruments in the emerging markets.
Ecuador, down 7.49 percent, underperformed all other countries in the EMBI-plus index in March.
"The rising interest rate environment and the poor prospects for economic reforms led to the sharp sell-off in Ecuadorian assets," it said.

For first-quarter results, Bulgaria took the lead, up 10.72 percent. Easing internal political tensions and progress in economic reforms were cited as contributing factors to Bulgaria's success, J.P. Morgan said.
In contrast, Ecuador was the worst performer in the first quarter, down 6.57 percent.
On a 12-month basis, Russia, up 107.81 percent, continues to lead the EMBI-plus index.

J.P. Morgan's Emerging Local Markets Index (ELMI), which tracks total returns for local-denominated money-market instruments, advanced 1.29 percent in March, generating a first quarter gain of 2.75 percent.
Unlike the EMBI+, J.P. Morgan said that all ELMI countries posted gains in March reflecting the diversification benefits that local currencies can provide in a global market downturn.

South Africa posted the best return for the third straight month, up 2.71 percent, according to the report. Argentina, up a modest 0.39 percent, was the worst performer as "excess liquidity in the banking system led to a decline in short-term rates," it said.
